newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Manley, legendary Caribbean politician, dead at 72.
newsitem.headline: Manley, legendary Caribbean politician, dead at 72.

text.p: Michael Manley, the former prime minister of Jamaica and a legendary figure in Caribbean politics, died after a long battle with prostate cancer, his family said on Friday. He was 72.

Manley died peacefully on Thursday night at his home in Kingston, according to a statement issued by his family. Diagnosed with cancer in 1990, he had been on life support since Wednesday and bedridden since December.

Son of the legendary Norman Washington Manley, who initiated Jamaica's two-party political system and was considered the father of the nation, Manley was prime minister during two of Jamaica's political eras.

In his early years in office, from 1972 until 1980, as Jamaica established itself as an independent nation, Manley espoused a fiery brand of Caribbean socialism and angered the United States with his close ties to the Communist government of Cuban President Fidel Castro.

His international reputation mushroomed as a champion of Third World causes, particularly in Africa, but Jamaica's worsening economic problems, food shortages and political violence cost him politically at home, and he was soundly defeated by the conservative Edward Seaga in 1980, an election so violent that it cost some 800 lives.

But Manley refashioned himself as a moderate, becoming an advocate of the free market and promoting a cooling of political violence. He was re-elected as prime minister in 1989, holding the office and continuing Seaga's economic reforms until health problems forced his retirement in 1992.
Eventually Manley would attend a White House dinner with U.S. President George Bush, who hailed him as an apostle of the free market system.

With news of his death, tributes poured in from colleagues, political opponents and world leaders. His archrival, Seaga, called him "a person of great personal charm" who may have articulated his views "stridently, even militantly, and certainly more actively" than many others, but was "smooth in argument and rich in laughter."
Prime Minister P.J. Patterson, Manley's main political protege, said he felt a "deep personal loss" at his death.
Patterson said his passing "marks the departure of a colossal figure" and internationally "people will grieve the loss of one who left an indelible mark" on the world scene.

Cuba called Manley's death a "sad loss" for the entire region. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Marianela Ferriol said the Cuban government would be sending a message of condolence to the Jamaican leader's family.

In a letter sent to Patterson, British Commonwealth Secretary-General Emeka Anyaoku said Manley was "a true believer in internationalism, he was a statesman of courage and conviction who extended his vision of a better and more just society beyond his island shores."

With the deaths of Manley and Guyana's President Cheddi Jagan, also on Thursday, the curtain closed on one of the most turbulent and politically active eras in Caribbean politics, political commentators said.
Manley was one of the signers of the treaty that created the Caribbean Community and was a leader in efforts to integrate the region's many scattered islands.

"I would say Michael Manley's greatest contribution to the region was that he helped to cement Caribbean unity and to establish a Caribbean Community," Edwin Carrington, secretary-general of Caricom, said.

Before dawn on Friday, a small crowd of well-wishers assembled at Jamaica House, the prime minister's office, to offer their condolences. The Jamaica Observer newspaper ran an unprecedented early morning second edition to announce "Manley is Dead."

Colleagues said that up to the very end, Manley was holding discussions with trade union leaders, political representatives and foreign investors on a wide range of issues. "The mind is there but the body is betraying me," Manley reportedly told friends just before he died.
Witty and articulate, Manley was the author of five books that covered his wide interests, including political ideology, the Jamaican bauxite industry and West Indian cricket.
He was married five times and had five children.
